Proto Northwest-Bahnaric *CV(C)ˈCV(C) is retained in Tariang but has become CV(C) in Kaseng, and vice versa. See examples in Table 9. ... Table 9: ... new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File check: (16 pp., text layer garbles IPA, so I rendered PDF p.2 = printed p.96 and PDF p.11 = printed p.105 and read the images). p.96: 'The language data given as examples are in broad phonetic transciption.' [sic] -- verbatim. p.105: 'As for cognate words, we detect the two different patterns of phonological changes: 1. Proto Northwest-Bahnaric *CV(C) ˈ CV(C) is retained in Tariang but has become CV(C) in Kaseng, and vice versa. See examples in Table 9.' -- verbatim (the printed stress mark has spaces around it). Table 9 ('Different patterns of phonological changes in Tairang [sic] and Kaseng'): Tariang kaˈlɛh 'egg', kaˈrias 'nail', taˈkool 'knee', caˈkɔɔŋ 'foot', maˈŋaaj 'person', ŋˈɲ…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Implicit, from first-hand phonetic transcription rather than a prose rule: Tariang words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables of the shape CV(C)ˈCV(C); in every sesquisyllabic form the author places the IPA stress mark before the final (main) syllable, i.e. the presyllable is unstressed and stress is word-final. This matches the explicit family-level description in Sidwell & Jacq 2003:33-34 ('a stressed mainsyllable is preceded by a minorsyllable... Sesquisyllabism is typical for Bahnaric'). No Talieng-specific sentence of the form 'stress falls on X' was found in any accessible source.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said; words are at most one minor + one main syllable in the data.
new_statements.exceptions: None. (1997:112 adds only that vowel length is not distinctive in Tariang.)
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms (isolated lexical items from fieldwork wordlists, Ban Dak Lan, Dak Chueng district); word-level; nothing on phrasal prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand data examined are Theraphan L-Thongkum's 'Tariang' recorded at Ban Dak Lan, Dak Chueng (Dakcheung) district, Sekong province, Laos (1997:111) = Glottolog tali1257 Talieng/Taliang [tdf]. Sidwell (2002:12 fn.3) states her Tariang 'is evidently the same language as Taliang discussed in Jacq & Sidwell 2000, and which we classified as a sister dialect of Kaseng'; Sidwell & Jacq (2003) treat 'Kasseng/Taliang' as one language (West Central Bahnaric). The 'Trieng' of the SIL Bangkok wordlist / Vietnamese Gie-Trieng [stg, Glottolog trie1243] is a different lect that patterns with West Bahnaric/Jeh-Halang (Sidwell 2002:12) and should not be conflated with tali1257.

sources.note: No prose rule. p.96: all data 'in broad phonetic transciption'; p.105: 'Proto Northwest-Bahnaric *CV(C)ˈCV(C) is retained in Tariang but has become CV(C) in Kaseng', Table 9 Tariang forms kaˈlɛh 'egg', kaˈrias 'nail', taˈkool 'knee', ʔaˈkuaj 'horn', ʔaˈkuan 'child' etc. -- the stress mark sits before the final (main) syllable in every sesquisyllabic Tariang form in the paper (also haˈpiat 'tongue', taˈpaaŋ 'palm', baˈhee 'otter').

sources.note: Talieng appears only in the Ethnologue classification list (p.590, 'WEST: Trieng, Talieng' under North Bahnaric); no StressTyp extract for it. Related Bahnaric extracts: Halang 'Stress is located on the final syllable'; Sedang 'Stress is located on the final, or the only, syllable' (p.592).

sources.citation: Sidwell, Paul & Pascale Jacq. 2003. A Handbook of Comparative Bahnaric, Vol. 1: West Bahnaric. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics (PL-551). hdl 1885/86178 (CC BY-SA 4.0).
sources.note: Family-level only, sec. 4.2 pp.33-34: 'Most WB languages are sesquisyllabic-a word may consist of one or one and a half syllables. In the latter case a stressed mainsyllable is preceded by a minorsyllable... Sesquisyllabism is typical for Bahnaric (and many other MK languages)'. Talieng is not West Bahnaric here (Kasseng/Taliang = 'West Central Bahnaric'); Kasseng/Taliang data cited from L-Thongkum 2001 ('TLT').

sources.note: Comparative/classificatory (c. 450 Tariang words collected Dec 1995 at Ban Dak Lan). No stress statement; Tariang forms consistently written with the stress mark before the final syllable (baˈdam 'five', taˈrɯw 'six', taˈpəh 'seven', kaˈcen 'nine', ʔaˈkuai 'horn', kaˈleh 'egg'); p.112 'Vowel length in Tariang is not distinctive.' (image-only PDF; tesseract scanned saved).
